papers.title: Lesion-Derived Estimated Functional and Structural Connectomes Predict Post-Stroke Recovery Outcomes
papers.abstract: Accurate prognosis after stroke remains challenging, limiting the ability to predict individual recovery. While advanced connectome MRI can provide further prognostically-useful information regarding affected brain networks, its impractical nature has given rise instead to lesion-based estimates of network disruptions. Here, we present a novel pipeline that leverages our recently developed connectome analysis tools to estimate structural disconnection (eSDC) and functional connectivity (eFC) directly from N=96 patient lesion masks for use in predicting motor, language, attention and memory outcomes at multiple timepoints after stroke. Our approach jointly leverages our Network Modification (NeMo) Tool, a database of white matter tractography results that estimates structural disconnectivity (eSDC), and the Krakencoder, a joint autoencoder that estimates functional connectomes (eFC) from the NeMo Tool's output. Models based on eSDC and eFC predicted almost all outcomes, particularly motor outcomes, significantly better than models that used patients' fMRI-based observed FC (oFC) and models based on only lesion information and covariates. Estimated connectome measures also i) retained meaningful inter-individual variability when compared to observed functional connectomes, ii) reflected population-level, stroke-related changes in functional connectomes, and iii) resulted in outcome prediction models with feature importances that aligned with expected networks of relevance to the given outcome. Feature importance analyses also identified distinct predictive signatures across both modality and outcome domain, indicating that eSDC and eFC capture non-redundant, biologically meaningful information about post-stroke network disruption. Together, these findings establish our lesion-based estimates of post-stroke structural and functional connectomes as a practical, information-rich alternative to advanced imaging in patients. This approach allows for probing an individual's affected neural circuitry underlying stroke impairment and recovery, paving the way toward more efficient, accessible, and personalized approaches to post-stroke prognosis and intervention.

papers.title: Chronic hypertension disrupts the blood-brain barrier in the ventral hippocampus in females but not males in a rat model of vascular cognitive impairment
papers.abstract: Background: Chronic hypertension is a leading cause of cerebrovascular disease, ischemic stroke, and cognitive impairment. In addition, anxiety and hypertension often co-exist, however, little is known about the relationship between the two. Understanding how chronic hypertension impacts limbic brain regions such as the ventral hippocampus may provide insight into how cerebrovascular contributes to altered emotional behavior. Methods: An open field task was used to quantify locomotion, exploratory behavior, thigmotaxis, rearing and risk assessment behaviors in adult (7-month-old) male and female normotensive Wistar rats and spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR; n=8/group). Blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability was assessed by measuring extravasation of sodium fluorescein, 3 kDa Texas red dextran and 10 kDa cascade blue into the ventral hippocampus. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays were used to measure markers of vascular signaling, inflammation, and central nervous system-specific proteins indicative of neuroaxonal and glial injury in serum from separate groups of male and female SHR (n=6/group). Main effects and interactions between two independent variables (sex and hypertension) were determined using two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey's post-hoc tests. Circulating factors were compared using a Welch's t-test. Relationships between BBB permeability and anxiety-like behavior were determined using Pearson's correlations. Results: Chronic hypertension increased circulating inflammatory factors and BBB permeability in female but not male rats. BBB permeability did not differ by sex in male and female normotensive rats. There was an anxiolytic effect of chronic hypertension on exploratory-related anxiety-like behavior, including less thigmotaxis, lower latency to cross through the center of the arena, and increased unsupported rearing. Risk assessment behavior, quantified as stretch-attend posture, was increased in female SHR. BBB permeability in the ventral hippocampus was correlated with anxiety-like behavior in females, but not in males, suggesting sex-dependent mechanisms of hypertension-induced changes in emotional behavior. Conclusions: These findings implicate a role for chronic hypertension-induced BBB disruption in neuropsychiatric disorders in the female sex and advances our understanding of cerebrovascular vulnerability in deep limbic brain regions.

papers.title: A Preventive Effect of Exercise in a Mouse Model of Essential Tremor
papers.abstract: The effects of exercise have not been widely studied for potential benefits in essential tremor (ET), while this has been growing for other neurodegenerative disorders. This study examines the effects of two types of exercise [high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and resistance training (RT)] on mice that were subjected to harmaline injections to trigger tremor. We employed a repeated-measures design with three groups: a HIIT group, a RT group, and a sedentary (SED) control group. Each group received an injection before and after the intervention. Tremor kinetics (power within the 8-14 and 14-29 Hz bands) were assessed using accelerometry. Tremor kinematics were also assessed using high-speed video analysis, for validation. As potential signalling molecules from exercise, we also tested for blood lactate and BDNF in each group. Compared to pre-intervention measurements, we found a significant decrease in power within the 8-14 Hz band combined with an increase in the 14-29 Hz band, for the HIIT group, but not in the RT or SED groups. We also found a change in BDNF concentration for the HIIT group. These results suggest that the HIIT protocol may have helped the animal to shift tremor frequency to higher bands, thereby offering functional resistance to harmaline-induced tremor. This study supports high intensity aerobic physical exercise as a potential therapeutic/preventive intervention for ET, with translational implications for human studies.

papers.title: Norepinephrine inhibits Afferent activation of NTS Catecholamine Neurons in Mice
papers.abstract: The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) integrates visceral sensory input to regulate feeding behavior, with catecholaminergic (CA) and neuropeptide Y (NPY)-expressing neurons playing key roles in energy homeostasis. Recent evidence suggests functional heterogeneity among CA-NTS neurons, including distinct subpopulations that either suppress or promote feeding. In this study, we investigated how norepinephrine (NE) modulates excitatory synaptic transmission from solitary tract (ST) afferents onto tyrosine hydroxylase-positive (TH) NTS neurons in mice. Using patch-clamp electrophysiology in horizontal brainstem slices, we found that NE inhibits ST-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (ST-EPSCs) in a concentration-dependent manner, with maximal effects at 10 microM and an EC of ~3.4 microM. This inhibition was mediated by alpha-adrenergic receptors and was independent of GABAA receptor activity. NE also suppressed asynchronous glutamate release and attenuated CCK-induced increase in spontaneous EPSC frequency, suggesting a presynaptic mechanism. NPY similarly reduced ST-EPSC amplitude via Y2 receptor activation, and co-application of NE and NPY produce additive or synergistic effects, even at subthreshold concentrations. Together, our results reveal a novel mechanism by which noradrenergic and peptidergic systems interact to regulate visceral sensory processing in the brainstem.

papers.title: Metabolic complexity in the human brain supports metastable network dynamics and declines in normative ageing
papers.abstract: The adaptive capacity of the brain is tied to the complexity of its neural activity. While entropy of brain signals has been used to characterise this complexity in haemodynamic and electrophysiological systems, it remains unknown whether entropy contributes to the temporal dynamics of the metabolic signals of the brain (glucodynamics) and how metabolic entropy may relate to network organisation, brain ageing and cognitive decline. Here, we combined dynamic functional PET (fPET) with 18F-fluoroedeoxyglucose and simultaneously acquired functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in 84 adults to investigate multiscale entropy (MSE) in the brain. We report that metabolic complexity measured with PET MSE represents non-linear, high-frequency complexity, whereas hemodynamic complexity reflects non-linearly constrained neurovascular phase dynamics. Greater metabolic complexity was associated with greater network metastability, particularly in unimodal and higher-order associative networks. Greater regional metabolic complexity also correlated with greater cortical thickness, cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (CMRglc) and cerebral blood flow, and was lower in older than younger adults. In contrast, global and network haemodynamic MSE was not significant associated with network dynamics. Higher global metabolic complexity was associated with better cognitive performance, and voxel-level derived MSE clusters were associated with cognitive performance in both modalities, with varied cluster sizes and spatial locations. However, these associations were largely accounted for by age variance. We conclude that temporal complexity in cerebral glucose is associated with the dynamics of the underlying metabolic signals, enables metastable network states and declines in ageing. Entropy of metabolic brain signals offers promise as a neurobiologically grounded metric of brain ageing.

papers.title: Differential effects of chronic hypertension and sex on vascular density along the septotemporal axis of the hippocampus in a rat model of VCID
papers.abstract: Background: Chronic hypertension is a major modifiable risk factor for vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID), yet vascular changes that precede cognitive dysfunction remain poorly understood. This is particularly relevant for the hippocampus, a deep brain structure critical to memory function, which differs along its septotemporal axis functionally and in its susceptibility to hypoxic/ischemic injury. The impacts of hypertension and sex on hippocampal vascularization remains unclear and could contribute to the development/progression of VCID. Methods: In this study, adult male and female Wistar and spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) were used at 5 months old, an age before memory impairments. Vascular density and morphometric parameters in dorsal and ventral hippocampus were quantified using high-resolution confocal microscopy and 3D vascular reconstruction. Results: In SHR, vascular density was increased in the dorsal hippocampus in males and across dorsal and ventral hippocampus in females compared to normotensive rats. Diameter and length of the microvasculature shifted to be smaller and longer during hypertension in males, but not females. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate chronic hypertension increases vascular density differentially by sex along the septotemporal axis of the hippocampus in mid adulthood that may increase vascular resistance and potentiate perfusion deficits or increase sites of blood-brain barrier disruption and contribute to VCID.

papers.title: Strategy-dependent causal relationships between large-scale cortical activity and perceptual decisions
papers.abstract: Animals can adopt different internally generated strategies to solve decision-making tasks, but whether cortical regions distinctly contribute to decisions under different strategies remains unknown. To address this problem, we analyzed three datasets comprising either cortical widefield imaging, or optogenetic inactivation of dozens of cortical locations in 54 mice, all performing the same sensory-evidence-accumulation task. Using Generalized Linear Model-Hidden Markov Models (GLM-HMMs), we found that the mice adopted one of three underlying strategies: an engaged, stimulus-driven state, and two disengaged states characterized by large side biases. The specific effects of inactivation of cortical regions depended on behavioral strategy: during engaged states, inactivation tended to increase side bias, while the opposite was true in biased states. For engaged states, these effects were most prominent when frontal regions were inactivated. Moreover, neural decoding analyses from cortex-wide activity revealed that frontal regions preferentially encode the animals' choices during engaged states relative to biased states. Our results suggest that distinct patterns of large-scale cortical dynamics underlie decisions under different task strategies and identify the frontal cortex as an important substrate of engaged-strategy control.

papers.title: Diagnose Harmonisation (DHARM): An open-source tool for the harmonisation and analysis of batch effects in MRI-derived measures.
papers.abstract: Technical differences between scanners, acquisition protocols, machine hardware and processing pipelines can introduce systematic variation into MRI-derived measures. Numerous harmonisation methods have been developed to reduce these effects. However, validation of these methods is often performed using different criteria depending on the method itself, the datasets used and the study design. Consequently, determining whether harmonisation is required, selecting an appropriate method and establishing whether or not technical variation has been sufficiently removed without compromising biological signal remain challenging. In this manuscript, we introduce Diagnose Harmonisation (DHARM), an open-source Python toolbox for diagnosing batch effects, applying harmonisation and evaluating harmonisation performance in cross-sectional and repeated-measures settings. DHARM is user-friendly, comes with GUI-based and command-line interfaces, and has graphical reporting. It provides standardised reporting workflows combining complementary measures of batch-associated differences in feature location, scale, empirical distributions, covariance and multivariate structure, together with measures assessing preservation of biological covariate effects and repeated-measures consistency. The framework includes several established harmonisation approaches, but its evaluation workflow is method-agnostic: users can also supply data harmonised using external or newly developed methods and benchmark their outputs using the same common set of diagnostics. We demonstrate DHARM using multisite cross-sectional MRI measures from UK Biobank, Cam-CAN and OxBAC as well as travelling-heads data from the ON-Harmony dataset. Across the cross-sectional datasets, harmonisation substantially reduced additive batch effects, while residual differences in variance and empirical distributions varied between methods. Multivariate diagnostics further demonstrated that reduction of batch-associated structure can coexist with preservation or increased detectability of biologically relevant variation. In the repeated-measures example, harmonisation reduced batch-associated and within-subject variability, while broadly preserving subject-level and biological relationships. DHARM provides a reproducible framework for diagnosing batch effects, applying different harmonisation methods and evaluating harmonisation as a multi-criteria problem rather than relying on a single measure of success. By jointly characterising technical variation and preservation of biologically meaningful information, DHARM can support dataset- and objective-specific selection, benchmarking and validation of harmonisation strategies.

papers.title: Self-Other Neural Representational Distinction is Associated with Distorted Social Predictions in Social Anxiety
papers.abstract: Background: Social anxiety (SA) is characterized by distorted negative expectations about the future. Because optimism bias is inherently comparative, the extent to which these predictions reflect a fundamental disruption in self- versus other-referential processing remains poorly understood. Methods: Across two experiments, we investigated the mechanisms underlying social predictions in SA. In Experiment 1, individuals with high (n = 52, LSAS > 65) and low SA (n = 51, LSAS < 35) rated the future likelihood of positive and negative social outcomes for themselves or for a protagonist. In Experiment 2, 35 adults spanning a continuous spectrum of SA completed the task during fMRI. Behavior was analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Neurally, multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) quantified self-other representational distinctions, while a parametric general linear model (GLM) tracked neural sensitivity to likelihood predictions. Results: Behaviorally, higher SA was characterized by an attenuated optimism bias: individuals predicted a lower likelihood of positive outcomes, but a higher likelihood of negative outcomes, for themselves compared to others. Neurally, higher trait SA correlated with greater self-other representational distinction within the left pregenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC). Concurrently, the precuneus exhibited stronger parametric tracking of self-negative predictions versus others. Crucially, pgACC representational distinction during positive outcome processing significantly mediated the association between SA severity and heightened prediction-tracking in the precuneus. Conclusions: These findings offer a novel mechanistic framework, suggesting that an exaggerated neural segregation of the self from others drives hyper-vigilant, risk-sensitive social predictions in SA. This candidate circuit-level dynamic warrants further replication in clinical cohorts.

papers.title: Fast rate coding in heterogeneous spiking networks
papers.abstract: A network of spiking neurons is said to operate in the rate coding regime if its dynamics can be accurately described by a continuous rate network. But how can discrete spike-based communication between neurons give rise to continuous rate-based dynamics? Computational studies showing that heterogeneous spiking networks can approximate the dynamics of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), a special case of rate network, assume that spikes are approximately Poisson or that network dynamics are slow. Here, we show that neither assumption is necessary: heterogeneous networks of non-Poisson neurons can produce fast rate-based dynamics. To demonstrate this, we show that signal transmission in feedforward networks of integrate-and-fire-type neurons can be described by a history-dependent rate network that is asymptotically exact as network size grows, even if heterogeneity persists, while linear-nonlinear rate networks fail. By providing a constructive model of fast rate coding in heterogeneous networks, this work lays the foundation for extending rate-based analyses of neural recordings beyond the assumption of slow dynamics or Poisson rate codes.

papers.title: Reducing the Risk of Gradient Induced EEG Hardware Heating During Simultaneous EEG-fMRI
papers.abstract: Simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional MRI (fMRI) has the potential to provide a more complete characterisation of brain function. Acquiring these data simultaneously requires the EEG hardware to be MR safe, since the EEG cap, amplifiers and powerpacks must be located within the MR environment. Placing them in this environment exposes them to both static and varying (radiofrequency (RF) and gradient) magnetic fields, presenting a potential heating risk. Previous studies have typically positioned the amplifiers and powerpacks outside of the bore, meaning that this risk is largely limited to the EEG cap. However, current guidelines recommend positioning the amplifiers within the bore. This reduces the distance between the EEG electrodes and amplifier, improving EEG signal quality and reducing risks of RF heating at the electrodes, but presents a potential heating risk for the amplifiers and powerpacks from the varying magnetic field gradients. In this study, we demonstrate that placing the amplifiers and powerpacks in the bore presents a significant heating risk, both at 7T and 3T. At 7T, we show that EPI sequences with a slew rate of at least 88 T/m/s resulted in significant heating of the EEG amplifiers. This heating effect could be negated by reducing the slew rate to 61 T/m/s. At 3T, we replicate the EEG amplifier heating and show that an alternative approach to reducing the gradient slew rates experience by the hardware is to increase the distance between the EEG amplifier/powerpacks and the isocentre of the magnet. Increasing the distance between the EEG hardware and MR isocentre by 30 cm mitigates the heating risk to the amplifiers and powerpacks, regardless of sequence parameters (e.g., slew rate). Therefore, whilst reducing the distance between the electrodes and amplifiers may improve EEG signal quality and reduce the potential for electrode RF heating, we show that risk of heating of hardware by gradient switching is greatly increased. This is particularly important to consider with the faster gradient slew rates available on modern MRI scanners, desired to increase spatial resolution. Experimenters must make careful decisions about hardware placement to ensure that the EEG-fMRI setup they use is safe, taking account of the varying risks that are posed by different approaches.

papers.title: APP functions at the endomembrane system
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: APP is a type I transmembrane protein, and its intracellular domain (AICD) interacts with FE65, X11, and mDAB1, et al., through the YENPTY motif. Accordingly, it has been proposed that the functions of APP are similar to Notch, which regulates gene expression through releasing NICD after combining with its ligands. However, the detailed underlying mechanisms of how FE65 is regulated by APP, as well as their target genes, remain unknown. METHODS: We overexpressed APP695 in N2a cells, and deleted/mutated APP in H4 cells by CRISPR-Cas9, respectively. The impacts of APP overexpression and ablation were detected by proteome comparison and immunoblotting. Thereafter, the subcellular localizations of APP and its binding protein FE65 were examined by immunofluorescence. RESULTS: APP overexpression not only resulted in its retention in Golgi apparatus (GA) and Endoplasmic reticulum (ER), but also induced FE65 clustering. In addition, it significantly reduced the protein level of ATF4 in N2a cells. On the contrary, knockdown of FE65 restored the protein level of ATF4. More importantly, APP overexpression also impaired autophagy. In contrast, knockout of APP rescued LC3 conversion. Of note, the APP Swedish mutant did not impact ER stress or the autophagic flux. Nevertheless, it facilitated the cleavage of APP-CTFs by gamma-secretase. DISCUSSION: The evidence presented in the current study demonstrates that APP is involved in stabilizing the endomembrane system and the subcellular transport of FE65. More importantly, the role of APP in regulating autophagy indicated that full-length APP could be considered a therapeutic target for preventing the development of AD.

papers.title: Stable large-scale network architecture and structured individual variability in the awake mouse brain
papers.abstract: Large-scale functional networks provide a scaffold for brain activity, but their population architecture and inter-individual variability remain poorly defined in the awake mouse brain. Here we introduce the Awake Mouse Connectome Project (AMCP), a population-scale multimodal MRI resource comprising 212 sex-balanced awake mice. Using this dataset, we generated high-precision in vivo tissue probability maps, derived a reproducible whole-brain functional network atlas and quantified structured variability in network connectivity across animals. The resulting atlas defined a stable large-scale architecture aligned with structural topology, while inter-individual functional connectivity variability followed organized connectional gradients rather than random dispersion. We further benchmarked the clustering-derived scaffold against conventional group independent component analysis (GICA) and release the GICA network atlas as an accompanying resource. AMCP further provides empirical scaling relationships linking sample size, scan duration and connectome precision. These analyses indicate that mean functional connectivity and functional connectivity variability have distinct sample-size requirements, providing a protocol-specific guidance for studies focused on group-average connectivity and inter-individual variability. Individualized network parcellations derived from the AMCP scaffold improved behavioural prediction relative to group-average features for selected behavioural domains, indicating functional relevance of subject-specific network architecture. Together, AMCP establishes an open dataset, tissue-template resource, clustering-derived and GICA functional atlases, and analysis toolbox for reproducible awake mouse connectomics and for translational studies linking circuit mechanisms to large-scale brain organization.

papers.title: Distinct processing of visual motion by transcriptomic cell types in the superior colliculus
papers.abstract: How the brain organizes visual processing across distinct neuron types is a fundamental yet unresolved question. Here we study how visual motion is processed by transcriptomically defined cell types in the superior colliculus (SC). We generated or identified transgenic mouse lines to target three transcriptomic types of neurons in the superficial SC, the Cbln4+, Vip+, and Grp+ neurons. We find that each of these cell types encodes distinct ranges of stimulus direction, speed, size, and spatial and temporal features. In response to ecologically relevant visual flows, the three cell types occupy partitional spaces in the encoding manifold. The three cell types also show unique morphology and connectivity, including their retinal and intracollicular input and projection patterns. Together, these results reveal a genetic logic for visual motion processing in the SC, where transcriptomic cell types are likely the basic computational units with their specific feature selectivity, morphology, and input-output connectivity.

papers.title: Evolution Shapes Cortical Interneuron Migration
papers.abstract: The cerebral cortex comprises excitatory neurons and inhibitory interneurons originating from distinct forebrain regions. During migration, cortical interneurons (cINs) interact dynamically with neighbouring cells and their microenvironment, contributing to cortical architecture. However, how evolutionary changes in cIN migration shape species-specific cortical development remains unclear. Comparative analyses in mouse, ferret, and human models revealed a conserved migratory sequence but distinct behaviours: human cINs migrate slower, display increased leading-process branching, and exhibit more frequent homotypic repulsive interactions than their mouse and ferret counterparts. These features promote dispersed cortical invasion of cINs in humans and ferrets, contrasting with the stream-like migration observed in mice. Mechanistically, elevated expression of the cytosolic carboxypeptidase CCP1 in human cINs reduces microtubule glutamylation and doublecortin recruitment, thereby facilitating leading-process branching. These findings identify a CCP1-dependent mechanism regulating cIN dispersion and suggest that evolutionary changes in cIN migration contribute to divergent patterns of cortical morphogenesis across mammals.

papers.title: Mapping brain networks underlying abstract perceptual decision formation and its EEG signatures
papers.abstract: Perceptual decisions have been proposed to involve a common mechanism of evidence accumulation operating across sensory modalities and motor contexts. In human EEG, the centroparietal positivity (CPP) tracks evidence accumulation in such a supramodal motor-independent manner, but its cortical sources are uncertain. Here we combined fMRI and EEG, acquired in separate sessions of the same supramodal change-detection paradigm, with individualized finite element head modeling to identify decision-related networks. A conjunction analysis across visual and auditory modalities and across motor and non-motor required tasks revealed consistent activation of bilateral postcentral, supramarginal, and superior parietal lobules, precentral gyrus, central operculum, middle frontal gyrus, and cerebellum. Forward modeling of fMRI-defined sources indicated that parietal-opercular regions were the dominant contributors to the response-locked and non-motor-required peak-locked CPP signal. These results implicate a network of brain areas in supramodal, motor-independent target-detection decisions, whose specific functional roles can be interrogated in more complex decision tasks in future.

papers.title: Structure-Based Discovery of GTP-Enhanced Rab10 Modulators and Their Effects on Alzheimer Disease-Relevant Cellular Phenotypes
papers.abstract: Rab10-mediated membrane trafficking has been implicated in Alzheimer disease (AD), but pharmacological tools for investigating its function remain limited. Here, we screened more than 80 million compounds using structure-based virtual screening and prioritized five candidate Rab10 modulators (R1-R5). These compounds exhibited favorable docking scores, stable modeled protein-ligand complexes in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and predicted acceptable ADME/toxicity profiles. Comparative docking against Rab5, Rab8, and Rab11 predicted preferential interactions with GTP-associated Rab10. R1 and R2 yielded the most favorable Rab10 scores, whereas R3 showed the largest differences between GTP-associated, GDP-containing, and nucleotide-free Rab10 models. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) revealed micromolar apparent affinities of R1-R4 without added GTP and nanomolar apparent affinities under GTP-containing conditions, generally favoring GTP-bound Rab10 over Rab5. In a cell-based GTP quantification assay, R1, R2, R3, and R5 reduced GTP-bound Rab10, whereas R4 increased it. R3 produced dose- and time-dependent reductions in GTP-bound Rab10 and was selected for functional studies. R3 altered endosomal organization and reduced EEA1 and LAMP1 expressions. In amyloid precursor protein (APP)/presenilin-1-expressing CHO cells, R3 redistributed intracellular APP, reduced APP carboxyl-terminal fragments (APP-CTFs), and decreased enlarged endosome-like structures. In neuronal differentiated PC12 cells, R1-R3 attenuated NGF withdrawal-induced cytoskeletal disruption and cell death, accompanied by reduced APP-CTF accumulation and tau phosphorylation. These studies highlight novel Rab10 modulators and support their further validation as candidate pharmacological probes for investigating Rab10-associated trafficking and AD-relevant cellular phenotypes.

papers.title: Brain mitovesicles undergo stage-specific remodelling during the progression of amyloid-β pathology
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is an early feature of Alzheimer's disease that shows nonlinear changes as the disease progresses. However, how these changes are reflected in the mitochondrial material released by brain cells remains poorly understood. Mitovesicles are a recently described extracellular vesicle subpopulation of mitochondrial origin that provide a unique insight into mitochondrial alterations in the brain and could potentially show how nonlinear changes evolve across disease stages of amyloid-beta pathology. Here, we isolated forebrain-derived small extracellular vesicles and mitovesicles from wild-type and Amyloid precursor protein (App) knock-in (AppKI) mice, carrying familial AD mutations and progressively accumulating amyloid-beta plaques, at presymptomatic (2-month) and symptomatic (12-month) stages using high-resolution density gradient fractionation. Vesicle identity and composition were assessed by morphological, biophysical and quantitative proteomic analyses, and mitovesicle respiratory function was measured by extracellular flux analysis. We show that mitovesicles carry a distinct, predominantly mitochondrial inner membrane proteome that is remodelled by age and disease in a stage-specific manner. Compared with small extracellular vesicles, mitovesicle proteomic profiles captured disease progression more clearly, with symptomatic AppKI mice forming the most molecularly distinct group. At the presymptomatic stage, AppKI mitovesicles showed reduced mitochondrial protein representation, most notably of fatty acid {beta}-oxidation and lipid-metabolism proteins associated with astroglial and vascular signatures, preceding any detectable respiratory impairment. At the symptomatic stage this reversed: AppKI mitovesicles were enriched for oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial membrane and transporter proteins, yet showed reduced Complex IV-linked respiration, revealing a dissociation between mitochondrial cargo abundance and respiratory function. Selected cargo changes were not mirrored in whole-brain tissue, indicating selective remodelling of mitovesicle content. Comparison with mitovesicles from post-mortem human Alzheimer's disease frontotemporal cortex and hippocampus identified a conserved 62-protein mitovesicle core, dominated by oxidative phosphorylation subunits and mitochondrial carriers. In addition, 25 of these proteins were enriched in mitovesicles derived from Alzheimer's and AppKI forebrains, defining a conserved mitovesicular disease signature. Together, these findings establish forebrain-derived mitovesicles as a dynamically remodelled vesicle population that reflects progressive mitochondrial dysfunction in the Alzheimer's disease brain and provides a cross-species resource for future biomarker and mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Spinal Noradrenergic Overdrive Promotes Reversible Motor Unit Aging and Sarcopenia
papers.abstract: Background Sarcopenia is characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical function with aging. Motor unit degeneration is a major contributor, but the mechanisms driving age-related deterioration of motor neurons, neuromuscular junctions (NMJs), and muscle fibers remain incompletely understood. Norepinephrine (NE) regulates spinal motor neuron excitability, but its role in motor unit aging has not been established. Methods Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology, optogenetics, fast-scan cyclic voltammetry, microdialysis, high-performance liquid chromatography, western blotting, and chemogenetics were used in mice aged 1-25 months. Motor neuron intrinsic properties were examined in 135 lumbar motor neurons from 81 mice. NE release dynamics, tissue content, and expression of the NE transporter (NET) and 2A-adrenergic autoreceptor were assessed in adult and aged mice. Descending spinally projecting noradrenergic neurons were selectively inhibited in aged mice using a retrograde chemogenetic approach. Results Aging produced progressive motor neuron hyperexcitability characterized by membrane depolarization, increased input resistance, elevated firing frequency, and altered action potential threshold (all P < 0.005). Optogenetically evoked endogenous NE increased motor neuron excitability by reducing action potential latency (P = 0.0001) and decreasing rheobase (P = 0.0028); these effects were prevented by 1-adrenergic receptor blockade (P = 0.0313). Aging enhanced stimulus-evoked spinal NE release, with greater responses at 20 Hz (P = 0.0223), 30 Hz (P = 0.0022), and 40 Hz (P < 0.0001). NE release elicited by stimulation of locus coeruleus and A5 noradrenergic inputs was also increased in aged mice (P = 0.0349 and P = 0.0016, respectively). Basal extracellular NE concentrations were unchanged, whereas spinal cord NE content increased (P = 0.0403). Aging reduced 2A-adrenergic receptor (P = 0.0009) and NET expression (P = 0.0046). Chemogenetic suppression of descending noradrenergic neurons in aged mice increased hindlimb muscle mass (P = 0.0111-0.0344), muscle fiber cross-sectional area (P = 0.0078-0.0467), NMJ innervation (P = 0.0210), and motor neuron soma size (P = 0.0353). Conclusions Aging promotes spinal noradrenergic overdrive characterized by increased NE storage, enhanced activity-dependent NE release, and impaired autoregulatory control. Excessive noradrenergic signaling contributes to motor neuron hyperexcitability and motor unit deterioration. Suppression of descending noradrenergic activity reverses structural features of motor neuron, NMJ, and skeletal muscle aging, identifying spinal noradrenergic signaling as a potential therapeutic target for sarcopenia.

papers.title: Closed-loop acoustic stimulation promotes local slow oscillation train initiation and persistence in elderly adults
papers.abstract: Slow oscillations (SOs) during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep support memory consolidation and metabolic waste clearance. Aging is associated with reduced SO amplitude and density and disrupted temporal organization, characterized by more isolated events and shorter SO trains. We investigated whether closed-loop acoustic stimulation (CLAS) could enhance the initiation and persistence of rhythmic SO activity in elderly adults. Twenty-seven participants underwent a baseline night followed by an experimental night, during which online-detected SOs were either stimulated using CLAS (STIM; n = 16) or left unstimulated (SHAM; n = 11). We quantified the proportions of isolated and consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and SO train length. Analyses assessed local effects around online-detected SOs and global effects across NREM sleep using offline detection. Locally, CLAS reduced the proportion of isolated SOs and increased the proportion of consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and mean train length. Global overnight effects were weaker but directionally consistent, primarily reflecting a shift toward longer SO trains. These changes occurred without a significant between-group difference in the change in SO density, and local effects remained significant after adjustment for SO density. Thus, CLAS promoted sustained rhythmic activity beyond changes in SO occurrence. These findings suggest that CLAS can modify the temporal organization of SOs in elderly adults, supporting its potential to mitigate age-related disruptions in SO dynamics. Temporal organization measures may complement conventional amplitude and density measures when evaluating CLAS effects. Further studies should establish whether these changes translate into cognitive benefits or improvements in other aspects of brain health.

papers.title: Parkinson Disease vs Aging Features Impairments in Formation and Release of a Power Grip in Real and Pantomimed String-Pulling
papers.abstract: Parkinson disease (PD) impairs skilled reaching tasks but less is known about its effects on rhythmic bimanual actions. We used a bimanual hand-over-hand string-pulling task that requires repeated reach, grasp, pull, push and release movements. We predicted that participants with PD would show impairment in making the rotary skilled hand movement of retrieving the string, analogous to impairments observed in single handed target reaching. Nine participants with PD (mean UPDRS-III: 24.6), 16 older adults, and 10 young adults successfully performed a real string-pulling task and then pantomimed the action. Video analyses combined optical-flow estimation of whole-body movement speed, markerless 2D pose estimation of upper-limb kinematics, and expert frame-by-frame scoring of hand and finger shaping. Machine-learning classification then identified the discriminative information carried by these multilevel movement components. Participants with PD showed lower movement speed, a smaller hand workspace, and reduced hand and finger shaping, with older adults showing intermediate values. All participants grasped the real string with a power grip, but participants with PD showed reduced rotary movements of the arm and the wrists and absent of arpeggio-like sequential finger movement during grasp and release. During pantomime, participants with PD moved faster and made larger hand movements, while grasp-related hand opening and finger sequencing was reduced or absent. The findings suggest that PD is expressed across this multicomponent movement manifold, and that the movement organization changes with task demands: real string pulling requires formation and release of a power grip, whereas pantomime does not place demands on grasping ability.

papers.title: Transcranial alternating current stimulation reverses adolescent alcohol-induced cellular and behavioral deficits.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alcohol is commonly consumed by adolescents in a binge-like pattern that can produce persistent cognitive impairments. Previous work found that adolescent intermittent ethanol (AIE) exposure reduces parvalbumin expressing (PV+) interneurons and increases perineuronal net (PNN) expression in brain regions critical for cognition. Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), a noninvasive neuromodulation technique, has shown promise for treating psychiatric disorders associated with cognitive dysfunction. Here, we examined whether AIE exposure alters PV+ interneurons and PNN expression in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and impairs cognition, and whether mPFC-targeted gamma tACS can reverse these effects. METHODS: Sprague Dawley rats (N=139, 50% female) underwent AIE or control exposure during adolescence and received Active or Sham mPFC-targeted gamma tACS treatment for three consecutive days in adulthood. Following stimulation, rats either underwent immunohistochemical assessment of PV+ and PNN expression or behavioral testing using the novel object recognition (NOR) task. RESULTS: AIE exposure reduced PV+ cell counts in the prelimbic cortex, an effect that was reversed by active tACS. In contrast, AIE exposure did not alter PNN measures. Interestingly, active tACS affected the prelimbic and infralimbic cortices more than the anterior cingulate cortex. AIE exposure also reduced recognition memory of a novel object, and this deficit was ameliorated by active tACS when assessed one week after stimulation. Additionally, active stimulation decreased anxiety-like behavior in the open-field test. CONCLUSIONS: Together, these results confirm that adolescent alcohol exposure produces lasting cellular and cognitive alterations and supports mPFC-targeted gamma tACS as a potential intervention for alcohol-induced dysfunction.

papers.title: Noise-referenced multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging for regional cerebrospinal fluid thermometry
papers.abstract: We developed a multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging approach for separate ventricular and subarachnoid cerebrospinal fluid thermometry. The approach uses measured image noise to assess agreement among temperature estimates. In 12 participants, temperature was estimated from four non-zero diffusion weightings. For each voxel, disagreement between these estimates was compared with that expected from image noise, accounting for their shared reference image. Voxels meeting this consistency criterion were retained for regional analysis. Mean diffusion-derived temperature ({+/-} SD) was 38.4 {+/-} 0.4 {degrees}C in the lateral ventricles and 36.0 {+/-} 1.1 {degrees}C in the subarachnoid space. Ventricular estimates were consistently higher than subarachnoid estimates across all participants, with a mean difference of 2.4 {+/-} 1.2 {degrees}C (95% confidence interval 1.6 -3.1 {degrees}C). This difference persisted under alternative noise models and temperature estimators. Subarachnoid estimates increased with retained voxel count; in a post hoc analysis of the six participants with the largest retained counts, ventricular estimates remained higher by 1.6 {+/-} 0.7 {degrees}C. Absolute temperature accuracy and the physiological origin of the regional difference require independent validation. This approach provides an internal consistency check for CSF thermometry and supports separate assessment of ventricular and subarachnoid temperatures.

papers.title: Graph neural network approach for inferring neuronal connectivity
papers.abstract: Understanding the connectivity of neuronal networks is essential for understanding brain function. Current anatomical mapping techniques, such as serial section microscopy and viral tracing, are resource-intensive and cannot capture the efficacy of connectivity. A complementary approach is to infer effective connectivity from single-neuron-resolution population activity. We developed a graph neural network (GNN)-based tool, CircuitGNN, that accurately infers neural effective connectivity from population activity. CircuitGNN accurately inferred the connectivity of several small circuits and detected both the strengthening and weakening of connections, such as those that occur during learning. CircuitGNN outperformed other methods when applied to simulated population activity generated by an invertebrate central pattern-generating circuit and a cortical microcircuit. CircuitGNN was evaluated on networks of varying size, recording duration, and proportion of hidden neurons. Although performance improved with longer recordings, CircuitGNN achieved high precision with recordings as short as 4 min, scaled to large circuits of up to ~750 neurons, and remained robust when 20% or 40% of neurons were hidden. These results establish CircuitGNN as an accurate and robust technique for inferring neural connectivity from activity.

papers.title: Brain-wide representations of olfactory behavior in C. elegans
papers.abstract: Olfactory navigation emerges from dynamic interactions between sensory input, brain activity state and the animal's own movements. In C. elegans, a compact nervous system enables brain-wide imaging in behaving animals exposed to controlled olfactory environments, with an undulatory locomotion that reduces navigation to transitions among forward runs, reversals, and turns. Here, we used tracking microscopy to record and compare brain-wide neural activity in crawling worms navigating spatial odor gradients or isotropic environments, and in immobilized worms responding to temporal odor pulses. Across conditions, we identified strongly correlated brain-wide activity patterns spanning olfactory sensory neurons, interneurons, and premotor interneurons. Comparisons between navigation in odor gradients and exploration in isotropic environments revealed a compact functional circuit linking olfactory sensory neurons, interneurons, and premotor neurons. Comparisons between different odors distinguished sensory activity relationships associated with odor identity from a shared sensorimotor circuit for navigational movement. Comparisons between crawling and immobilized animals revealed profound differences in motor-state transitions and brain-wide correlation structure, further demonstrating the dependence of sensory representations and motor decision-making on behavioral context. Our findings reveal a functional organization linking olfactory sensory activity to navigational movement and show how this organization depends on behavioral state and environmental context.

papers.title: Hmox1/CO regulates retina regeneration via modulation of Wnt/β-catenin signalling and induction of vaspb in zebrafish
papers.abstract: Muller glia (MG) in the zebrafish retina retain a latent stem cell capacity that is absent in mammals, yet the injury responsive signals that drive this reprogramming remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify heme oxygenase-1 (Hmox1), the stress-inducible, rate-limiting enzyme of heme catabolism, as a previously unrecognized regulator of this process. Following injury, hmox1a is selectively and rapidly induced among the heme oxygenase gene family, localizing to photoreceptors with expression peaking during the MG proliferation window. Pharmacological inhibition and morpholino mediated knockdown of Hmox1 dysregulate the acute inflammatory response, impair Muller glia-derived progenitor cell (MGPC) proliferation, and produce lasting deficits in retinal lamination, establishing Hmox1 as a potentially non-redundant, early-acting node required for structural recovery. Exogenous delivery of carbon monoxide (CO), a bioactive Hmox1 metabolite, partially rescues each of these phenotypes, functionally implicating CO as a key downstream effector. Mechanistically, Hmox1/CO signalling stabilizes {beta}-catenin likely via transcriptional repression of the Wnt antagonist dkk1b. This stabilized {beta}-catenin is enriched at a predicted Tcf7l2 site in the promoter of vaspb, which encodes an actin binding protein and is newly identified here as an injury-induced Wnt target gene. Bioinformatic and functional analyses further implicate Nfe2l2a (Nrf2) as a candidate intermediary bridging Hmox1/CO to Wnt regulation, with putative antioxidant response elements identified within the dkk1b locus. Together, these findings outline a putative Hmox1[->]CO[->]Nrf2[->]dkk1b[->]{beta}-catenin[->]vaspb relay coupling redox biology to Wnt-dependent glial reprogramming. Notably, HO-1 is similarly induced in stressed mammalian retina, yet Wnt/{beta}-catenin activation fails to sustain regeneration, positioning the Hmox1/CO axis as a candidate target for future investigation in mammalian retina regeneration.

papers.title: NeuralFieldManifold: Uncovering the Manifold Geometry of Local Field Potentials
papers.abstract: Manifold geometry has become a powerful framework for understanding how the brain organizes high-dimensional neural activity into compact, interpretable structure. To date, however, most theoretical and methodological advances in neural manifold analysis have focused on spiking activity, leaving unresolved a fundamental question: What are the geometric principles governing the dynamics of local field potentials (LFPs); population level signals reflecting integrated subthreshold and suprathreshold neural activity that are broadly integral to clinical and brain-computer interface settings. Here, we establish, analytically and empirically, that the lag-embedded dynamics of LFP signals lie on a low-dimensional K-torus, where K directly relates to sustained oscillatory modes present in the signal. Modeling LFPs as bounded autoregressive processes, we show that each oscillatory component contributes an independent circular degree of freedom, while aperiodic 1/f structure and noise contribute only geometric thickness around the manifold without altering its topology. To apply this theory to real nonstationary recordings, we introduce DeepLagField, a physics-informed network that jointly estimates time-varying AR structure and effective model order, with formal guarantees that local toroidal geometry is preserved despite non-stationary nature of neuronal processes. Persistent homology analysis on real recordings reveals topological signatures consistent with the predicted toroidal Betti numbers in primate V1 LFP, rodent hippocampal LFP, and mouse cortical EEG, with varying degrees of agreement across recordings and temporal windows. Crucially, decoding analyses across three distinct neural datasets demonstrate that these geometric structures are not merely descriptive but capture behaviorally relevant information rivaling conventional spectral features. Together, these findings establish a theoretically grounded and empirically validated geometric framework for neural field analysis, extending the manifold perspective beyond spiking activity and offering a complementary language to spectral analysis for understanding and translating population dynamics across neural modalities.

papers.title: Imipramine binds to amyloid-β and extends the survival of Alzheimer's disease patients
papers.abstract: Background Apolipoprotein E (apoE) plays numerous roles in the pathogenic pathway to Alzheimer's disease (AD). We previously performed a high-throughput screen and identified the antidepressant imipramine as an inhibitor of the interaction between apoE and amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}). We also found that imipramine use to treat depression in AD patients was associated with better Mini-Mental State Exam (MMSE) scores. Here we studied the mechanisms by which imipramine inhibits the AD pathogenic pathway and investigated its effect on mortality in AD patients. Methods Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy was used to characterize the interaction between imipramine and A{beta} monomers. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived AD cerebral organoids (COs) and transgenic AD rats treated with imipramine underwent neuropathological evaluation, while rat learning and memory were assessed in the Morris Water Maze. AD patient mortality in the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center's database was analyzed by Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards models. Results Imipramine inhibits the apoE-A{beta} interaction by binding directly to A{beta} monomers. Imipramine reduces A{beta} accumulation and neuronal cell loss in AD COs. Imipramine-treated female AD rats had enhanced reference memory and increased hippocampal cellularity and cholinergic neurotransmission. AD patients prescribed imipramine had reduced all-cause mortality over 10 years relative to those prescribed other tricyclic antidepressants (TCA), non-TCA antidepressants, or no antidepressants. Conclusions The findings support the conclusions that: a) the mechanism by which apoE confers risk for AD is by catalyzing the polymerization of A{beta} into neurotoxic species, b) targeting apoE is a promising, underappreciated strategy for the prevention of AD, c) imipramine should be used more frequently to treat depression in AD clinical practice, and d) imipramine should be evaluated in prospective trials, particularly in APOE4 carriers, as a potential method to improve cognition and reduce mortality in AD.

papers.title: Paraquat Inhalation Produces Male-Biased Dopaminergic Neuron Loss and Motor Deficits in Mice: Relevance to Parkinsons Disease
papers.abstract: Long-term exposure to paraquat (PQ), a widely used herbicide, has been linked to increased risk of Parkinsons Disease (PD) in agricultural workers and rural communities in the United States (US), findings further supported by experimental animal studies. Although banned in many countries across the globe, PQ remains widely used in the US. Inhalation of PQ has been known to induce systemic organ failure at acute concentrations. However, prolonged low-dose inhalation from agricultural spraying and pesticide drift has not been readily evaluated for its potential to contribute to neurodegenerative diseases in vivo. Instead, many experimental studies have relied on systemic routes of exposure, which do not effectively replicate the most common route of exposure to PQ in the environment. In the current study, Parkinsonian features were examined in mice that had been exposed via whole-body inhalation to PQ aerosol for either 40 or 60 days. Levels of PQ in brain were highest in olfactory bulb, followed by frontal cortex and then brainstem in both sexes. After 60 days of exposure, male-specific impairments in locomotor activity were observed, in addition to reductions in striatal dopamine, in substantia nigra tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression and number of TH+ dopaminergic neurons, the latter being considered the primary basis of PD, along with increased olfactory bulb -synuclein levels. As such, these studies confirm the dopaminergic neurotoxicity of inhaled PQ. These findings raise significant concerns as to the contribution of PQ exposures to the continued increase in the incidence of PD in the US.

papers.title: Pubertal timing is a critical dimension of adolescent brain vulnerability
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a period of rapid brain development, during which biological maturational timing varies substantially between individuals. This variability may drive specific developmental vulnerabilities to adverse experiences with long-term consequences, warranting early identification of at-risk individuals. We utilized ultrasonic bone age measurements to track pubertal maturity, classifying participants by adolescent biological maturity relative to chronological age (accelerated, average, decelerated). Brain hierarchy was quantified as the irreversibility of brain signals in resting state electroencephalography, providing a brain-based method to detect vulnerability patterns. The COVID-19 pandemic presented a unique opportunity to also assess alterations in brain hierarchy following external disruption. We mapped maturity-defined trajectories and rates of hierarchical organization, and their post-pandemic deviation from expected development, capturing two distinct vulnerability forms. First, early maturing adolescents showed persistent reduction in brain hierarchy. Second, those undergoing their fastest phase of development - specifically, decelerated adolescents - showed the strongest disruption in brain hierarchy following the pandemic. These findings suggest that pubertal timing is a critical dimension of individual variation in adolescent brain development and vulnerability. They also emphasize the need for objective maturity measurements to tailor support to individual pubertal timelines, particularly given the secular trend toward earlier puberty and ongoing global ecological crises.
